title: Spring Boot 3.5.0 to 4.1.1 on Java 21
summary: This moves the employee service from Spring Boot 3.5.0 to 4.1.1 and from Java 17 to Java 21. Boot 4 brings Jackson 3, Spring Framework 7, Spring Security 7 and Hibernate 7 with it, so a handful of source files have to change even though no business logic does. The code graph shows only six of the seventeen types touching anything defined outside the repository, and those are the files this plan predicts will break — the other eleven never name a framework type at all. The seven REST endpoints are expected to answer identically afterwards, and five probes replayed on both runtimes will show whether that held. Best estimate is six build rounds over about half a day; the least certain part is the test layer, which cannot even be compiled until the main code is clean.
drivers: Spring Boot 3.5.x leaves open-source support in mid-2026; security patches after that are commercial-only.
Java 21 is the LTS the Boot 4 generation is built and tested against.
Jackson 2.x, pulled in transitively today, has no fix branch for the deserialization advisories tracked against it.

architecture_reading.summary: The graph shows a single Maven module with 17 types, one controller exposing 7 endpoints, and 12 declared dependencies. Only 6 types extend or implement something defined outside the repository, and 2 of those 6 extend java.lang.RuntimeException, which no framework jump can touch. That leaves four real framework touchpoints — the health indicator, the exception handler, the JPA repository and the startup runner — and they are where the compiler is expected to fail.
framework_coupling: `DatabaseHealthIndicator` implements `HealthIndicator`, an external type. The actuator health contract is one of the packages Boot 4 relocates, so this is the highest-confidence prediction in the plan.

`GlobalExceptionHandler` extends `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` and carries `@RestControllerAdvice`. It sits directly on the Spring Framework 7 boundary and owns the error contract every 4xx probe checks.
`EmployeeRepository` extends `JpaRepository` — Hibernate 7 comes with the jump, so this is where a persistence-layer signature change would surface.

`EmployeeController` scores highest for exposure (16): `@RestController` plus `@RequestMapping` plus all 7 endpoints. Nothing about it is expected to change, but it is where a regression would be most visible.
`JacksonConfig` is one of two `@Configuration` types and is the only one that builds an ObjectMapper, so the Jackson 2 to 3 change is contained to it.
blind_spots: The graph has no edges for `application.yml`, so property renames between generations appear nowhere in it — those surface at runtime, not at compile time.
The Dockerfile base image and the CI workflow's Java version are ancillary files the graph does not model; both were read from baseline.json instead.
One description in the graph is marked stale, so the semantic layer has drifted since it was written and criticality is reported as unknown throughout.
The graph covers main source only. The three test classes were read from disk, which is why the test-layer estimate is the softest number here.

phases.name: Build file and coordinates
phases.goal: Move the parent, the language level and the renamed starters, and let the resolver say what no longer exists.
expected_failures: Unresolvable artifacts where Boot 4 split or renamed a starter
Missing packages where Jackson 2 types were imported
graph_evidence: The graph lists 12 declared dependencies on this module, 6 of them Spring Boot starters the reference pack flags as renamed or split.

phases.name: Main source — health, error handling and JSON
phases.goal: Follow the compiler through the relocated packages until main compiles.
expected_failures: The actuator health package no longer resolves in DatabaseHealthIndicator
ResponseEntityExceptionHandler's overridable signatures changed under Framework 7
ObjectMapper configuration methods that no longer exist on the Jackson 3 type
graph_evidence: Exactly 3 types hold the framework touchpoints this phase covers: DatabaseHealthIndicator (implements HealthIndicator), GlobalExceptionHandler (extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler) and JacksonConfig (@Configuration).

phases.name: Test layer
phases.goal: Bring the tests onto the new test starters and mocking annotations. Tests only compile once main does, so this cannot start earlier.
expected_failures: Removed test annotations in the three test classes
Mapper type mismatches in the controller test
Testcontainers integration test failing on a changed JDBC or Hibernate default
graph_evidence: The graph covers main source only, so this phase is sized from the three test files on disk rather than from measured coupling.

predicted_changes.what: Parent to 4.1.1, java.version to 21, renamed starters.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 splits spring-boot-starter-web by stack and modularises the test starters.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The graph's DEPENDS_ON edges list all 12 declared coordinates for this module.

predicted_changes.what: Import and implement the relocated HealthIndicator/Health types.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 moves the actuator health contract to a new package root.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The only type in the graph with an IMPLEMENTS edge to the external type HealthIndicator.

predicted_changes.what: New Jackson 3 package root and mapper builder API.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 carries Jackson 3, which changes the package root and the configuration entry point.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: One of two @Configuration types and the only one that constructs a mapper.

predicted_changes.what: Update the overridden handler signatures to the Framework 7 shapes.
predicted_changes.why: ResponseEntityExceptionHandler's protected methods changed with Spring Framework 7.
predicted_changes.reference_rule: 11. Verify a coordinate or class before using it
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: Extends the external type ResponseEntityExceptionHandler; exposure score 4.

predicted_changes.what: Replace the removed test annotation and update the health assertions.
predicted_changes.why: The test annotation it uses is removed in Boot 4 and the health document's shape changed with the package move.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: Not in the graph (main source only) — read from disk alongside the health indicator it exercises.

predicted_changes.what: New mocking annotation and Jackson 3 mapper type.
predicted_changes.why: Boot 4 retires the old mock-bean annotation and the test's mapper type moves with Jackson.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: Exercises EmployeeController, the highest-exposure type in the graph (score 16).

predicted_changes.what: Base image to a Java 21 JRE.
predicted_changes.why: The language level moves to 21, so the runtime image has to carry a JDK that can run the artifact.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: Not modelled in the graph — listed in baseline.json's ancillary files.

predicted_changes.what: Possibly a renamed actuator or Jackson property.
predicted_changes.why: Property renames between generations do not appear at compile time and only surface when the application starts.
predicted_changes.graph_evidence: The graph has no configuration edges at all, so this is a reference-pack prediction with nothing measured behind it.

dependency_plan.reason: The generation jump itself — every managed version underneath follows from this one.
The LTS the Boot 4 generation is built and tested against.
Boot 4 splits the web starter by stack; this application is servlet-based.
The test starter is modularised in Boot 4; the pieces the tests actually use are declared explicitly.

risks.risk: The actuator health document changes shape, so anything scraping /actuator/health sees a different payload even though no application code changed.
risks.mitigation: The health endpoint is in the probe list and its body is compared before and after; any difference is reported as a client-visible change rather than rounded down to unchanged.
risks.graph_evidence: DatabaseHealthIndicator contributes to that endpoint and is one of the types that must change.

risks.risk: A configuration property is renamed, so the application compiles and starts but behaves differently.
risks.mitigation: The readiness check plus five endpoint probes run against the actually-started application on the new runtime, not just against the build.
risks.graph_evidence: The graph has no configuration edges, so nothing in the round loop would ever surface this.

risks.risk: Spring Security 7 changes a default and the 401 boundary answers differently.
risks.mitigation: An unauthenticated request is one of the five probes and is checked for exactly 401, not merely for not-200.
risks.graph_evidence: SecurityConfig carries @EnableWebSecurity and is one of only two @Configuration types in the graph.

risks.risk: The Testcontainers integration test fails on a Hibernate 7 default rather than on the migration.
risks.mitigation: Round 0 records the test suite passing on the old runtime, so a test that fails only after the jump is attributable; every round is kept for comparison.
risks.graph_evidence: EmployeeRepository extends JpaRepository — the only persistence touchpoint in the graph.

risks.risk: The test layer needs more work than forecast and the migration stalls after main compiles.
risks.mitigation: The test phase runs its own rounds with package, and every round is recorded — a stall is visible in the ledger rather than hidden.
risks.graph_evidence: The graph covers main source only, so the test-layer estimate is the least evidence-backed number in this plan.

behaviour_plan.summary: The same five requests are replayed against the running application on Java 17/Boot 3 before anything changes and on Java 21/Boot 4 once the build is green. Status codes must match exactly; a body that differs with the same status is judged and explained rather than assumed benign.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees
probes.why: The happy path and the shape of the collection response.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees/1
probes.why: Single-resource serialization — the most likely place a Jackson change shows.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees/99999
probes.why: The error contract, owned by GlobalExceptionHandler, which is itself changing.

probes.name: GET /api/v1/employees (no auth)
probes.why: The authentication boundary — Spring Security 7 comes with the jump.

probes.name: GET /actuator/health
probes.why: The endpoint whose implementation is being changed.

not_covered: The three write endpoints (POST, PUT, DELETE) are not probed — they write, and the probe run has no way to undo itself.
No scheduled or background work exists in this application, so nothing time-driven is checked.
Load and latency are not measured — the probes prove the contract, not the performance.

effort.estimated_duration: about half a day, assuming both JDKs are installed and the first BOM download is not counted

rollback: Nothing in the project changes until the very last step. If the applied result is bad, `node scripts/apply-migration.js --slug spring-boot-3-to-4 --revert` restores every overwritten file from the pre-apply backup.
out_of_scope: No refactoring, renaming or reformatting — the diff should contain only what the upgrade forced.
No unrelated dependency bumps; a library that resolves fine under Boot 4 is left at the version it is on.
No change to the database schema or to the seed data.
The one stale graph description is not refreshed as part of this — that belongs to 01b-context-weaver.
open_questions: Is 4.1.1 the release you want, or should this wait for the next patch?
The health document's shape is expected to change — is anything on your side parsing it that we should warn first?
The three write endpoints are not probed because the run cannot undo itself. Is that acceptable, or should the migration set up a disposable database for them?
